sentences.text: He found the box on the eleventh of December, under the hedge at the bottom of the yard, and he found it by putting his hand somewhere he should not have put his hand.
The hedge at the bottom was thick at the base and full of the things hedges are full of.
He was after a ball that had gone under, and he was flat on the wet ground with his arm in up to the shoulder, and his fingers came down on a corner that was flat and dry and cardboard.
It took him a long time to get it out.
It was further in than his arm went and he had to fetch the rake and work it sideways.

While he was working it out he found four other things, which is what happens under a hedge: half a tennis ball, a fork, a plastic dinosaur that had been his when he was about six, and a great quantity of leaves that had been leaves for a very long time.
None of them were dry.
It was a shoebox.
Green, with a brand on the side that had not existed for twenty years, and it was not damp, which under a hedge in December is not a thing a shoebox can be.
He sat back on his heels in the wet and took the lid off.
The box was full of evenings.

He has never worked out how to describe this and he has stopped trying, so what he says now is simply what he saw, which is that the box contained nine flat pieces of light about the size of a postcard, lying on top of each other like slides, and every one of them was the last hour of a day.
You could see into them.
Not a picture — a picture is flat and this was not flat, it had a distance in it.
He looked into the top one and there was the back yard from the height of his own eyes and the sky going orange behind the depot and the sound, faintly, of his aunt on the telephone in another room.
The second one down was a different evening.
There was rain on it.
He went through all nine, kneeling in the mud with the lid beside him, holding each one up to what was left of the daylight.
Three of them had rain.
One had the smell of somebody burning garden waste two gardens over, which he remembered and had not thought about since.
One was almost entirely dark and had a single lit window in the top corner, which he worked out after a while was the Ferreiras' landing.
And every one of them was the yard.
Every single one was that view, from that height, from the back door — as though somebody had stood in exactly his place on fourteen separate evenings and had not moved.
He put the lid back on because his hands had started to shake, and he sat in the mud at the bottom of the yard with a shoebox on his knees for a while, and then he heard the noise.

It was a snuffling, industrious, entirely un-mysterious noise, coming from under the hedge about a metre to his left, and it was the noise of a hedgehog who has been interrupted and is deciding whether to be bothered about it.
